translationRepairs: When the founding ancestor Li Guochang first submitted to the Tang court, Emperor Xianzong granted the family a residence in Qinren Ward. From the Changqing reign onward, a member of the clan in each generation held command of the palace guard.

When the Virtuous Ancestor (Yizu) first submitted to the Tang court, Emperor Xianzong granted the family a residence in Qinren Ward. From the Changqing reign onward, a member of the clan in each generation held command of the palace guard.
Focus unit names 懿祖, not 國昌; the prior idiomatic invents Li Guochang. Virtuous Ancestor (Yizu) correctly renders the temple name while leaving the rest of the sentence intact.
Early in the Dazhun era, after the Lu commander Ke Xiu died, Ke Gong succeeded him as military commissioner of Zhaoyi.
Early in the Dashun era, after the Lu commander Ke Xiu died, Ke Gong succeeded him as military commissioner of Zhaoyi.
大順 is the Tang era name Dashun; Dazhun is a romanization error with no support in the Chinese.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month Ke Gong went to visit the wounded Yuanshen at the home of the clerical officer Liu Chongzhi.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month Ke Gong went to visit the wounded Yuanshen at the home of the clerical officer Liu Chong.
劉崇之第 is Liu Chong's residence: 之 is the possessive marker and 第 means residence, so Liu Chongzhi is an invented personal name.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, Ke Gong visited Yuanshen at the residence of the clerical officer Liu Chongzhi.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, Ke Gong visited Yuanshen at the residence of the clerical officer Liu Chong.
The same 劉崇之第 construction governs the literal field; Liu Chong is the officer and 之第 marks his residence, not a given name Chongzhi.

The historiographer writes: The Martial Emperor rose from the Yin Mountains and Emperor Zhuangzong founded his rule in Hebei. Though they briefly held the realm, their dynasties were short-lived. Their kinsmen bloomed like catalpa blossoms yet bore no fruit—they never attained Emperor Yao's generous ordering of kin or the enfeoffment principles of King Guangcheng.

The historiographer writes: The Martial Emperor rose from the Yin Mountains and Emperor Zhuangzong founded his rule in Hebei. Though they briefly held the realm, their dynasties were short-lived. Their kinsmen bloomed like catalpa blossoms yet bore no fruit—they never attained Emperor Yao's generous ordering of kin or broadly extended King Cheng's principles of enfeoffment.
廣成王封建之義 parallels 推帝堯敦敘之恩: 廣 is the verb matching 推, and 成王 is King Cheng, not a fused royal name Guangcheng.

The historiographer remarks: In former times the Martial Emperor rose from the Yin Mountains and Emperor Zhuangzong founded his rule in Hebei. Though they briefly held all under Heaven, their enjoyment of the realm was brief. Turning affection to the branch kin, the flowering of the catalpa alone was empty show. They indeed did not reach the point of extending Emperor Yao's generous ordering of kin, or King Guangcheng's principle of enfeoffment.

The historiographer remarks: In former times the Martial Emperor rose from the Yin Mountains and Emperor Zhuangzong founded his rule in Hebei. Though they briefly held all under Heaven, their enjoyment of the realm was brief. Turning affection to the branch kin, the flowering of the catalpa alone was empty show. They indeed did not reach the point of extending Emperor Yao's generous ordering of kin, or of broadly extending King Cheng's principle of enfeoffment.
Literal likewise misread 廣成王 as one name; the repair restores the parallel verbs 推/廣 and the referent 成王 as King Cheng.
From Ke Rang downward, none received fiefs like the states of Lu and Wei, nor did they show the virtue of Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou.
From Ke Rang downward, none received fiefs like the states of Lu and Wei, nor did they cultivate the virtue of the Princes of Hejian and Dongping.
懋間、平之德 pairs with 魯、衛之封 as exemplary imperial kin: 間 and 平 are the Han princes of Hejian and Dongping, not Zhou Kings Wen and Wu.
From Ke Rang downward, they did not obtain enfeoffment like Lu and Wei, nor did they display the virtue of the Zhou kings Wen and Wu.
From Ke Rang downward, they did not obtain enfeoffment like Lu and Wei, nor did they display the virtue of Jian and Ping (the Princes of Hejian and Dongping).
The literal's Zhou Wen and Wu reading has no basis in 間、平; Jian and Ping as the Princes of Hejian and Dongping matches the Chinese allusion.
